title: Cloudflare beats Q2, raises 2026 guidance, and points to AI-agent traffic as the reason
subtitle: August 7 results — $696M revenue up 36% year over year, EPS of $0.29 versus $0.27 consensus, full-year outlook lifted to $2.864B–$2.870B — added Cloudflare to the small group of listed companies whose top line now visibly moves with AI infrastructure demand.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Cloudflare reported second-quarter revenue of $696.1 million on August 7, up 36% from the same period a year earlier, beating the $664.7 million analyst consensus. Adjusted EPS came in at $0.29 versus $0.27 expected. The company raised its full-year 2026 revenue guidance to $2.864 billion to $2.870 billion from a prior range of $2.805 billion to $2.813 billion, and lifted its full-year adjusted EPS outlook to $1.25 to $1.26 from $1.19 to $1.20. Current remaining performance obligations rose 35%. Shares closed up roughly 8% on the day after trading as much as 16% higher in the premarket. Management attributed the beat and the guidance raise to enterprise demand for AI infrastructure — routing, securing, and serving AI-agent traffic across its network — rather than to core CDN growth.

The specific line item worth watching is AI-agent traffic. Cloudflare sits at a peculiar chokepoint: it operates the network layer that both hosts a large fraction of the sites AI agents want to visit and, increasingly, hosts the agents themselves through Workers, Browser Run, and the newly announced Kitesurf browser engine. That double-sided position means Cloudflare gets paid on both ends of an agent interaction — once by the publisher for bot management and rate-limiting, once by the agent operator for the runtime. It is one of the few businesses where you can already read the AI capex boom in the revenue line rather than only in the capex line. Nvidia has the same property on the hardware side; Cloudflare is a rare software-side analogue.

The broader signal is that AI infrastructure spend is now large enough and recurring enough to show up in the quarterly numbers of adjacent companies, not just at the labs themselves. That was not obviously true a year ago, when most AI revenue was concentrated at OpenAI, Anthropic, the hyperscalers, and Nvidia. The Q2 2026 print from Cloudflare, alongside AMD's 50% year-over-year revenue jump to $11.5 billion and its Taalas acquisition earlier in the week, suggests the second tier of AI-adjacent public companies — networking, edge compute, security — is starting to see structural, not cyclical, demand. Whether that continues depends on whether AI-agent traffic follows the trajectory of previous traffic-class booms (video, mobile) or plateaus once the initial wave of agent deployments is done.

For learners: earnings calls are an underused source of ground truth about what is actually happening in AI. Labs and vendors have every incentive to describe their business as growing; adjacent companies have every incentive to describe it accurately, because their own guidance depends on getting the trajectory right. If you want a cheap and reliable way to track AI adoption, read the Q&A sections of the Cloudflare, Fastly, Snowflake, Datadog, and Palo Alto Networks quarterlies. The prepared remarks are marketing; the questions from equity analysts are usually the interesting part.
